To inject secrets into an application running in a Kubernetes Pod using the Vault sidecar (Vault Agent Injector), you typically follow these steps:

### 1. Prerequisites
- Deploy Vault and set up the [Vault Kubernetes Auth method](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/auth/kubernetes).
- Set up the Vault Agent Injector - an admission webhook that injects the sidecar.

### 2. Write a Vault Policy & Role

**Policy:**
```hcl
path "secret/data/myapp/config" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
```

**Role (CLI):**
```bash
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/myapp-role \
  bound_service_account_names=myapp-sa \
  bound_service_account_namespaces=default \
  policies=myapp-policy \
  ttl=1h
```

### 3. Annotate Your Pod or Deployment for Injection

Add the following annotations at the Pod template level (deployment or directly in a pod YAML):

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: myapp
  annotations:
    vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"
    vault.hashicorp.com/role: "myapp-role"
    vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-config: "secret/data/myapp/config"
spec:
  serviceAccountName: myapp-sa
  containers:
    - name: myapp
      image: myapp:latest
```

- The `agent-inject-secret-<name>` annotation creates a file named `<name>` under `/vault/secrets/<name>` in the pod, containing the secret value.

The following explanation assumes that you already have Vault running and configured to talk to your Kubernetes cluster.

──────────────────────────────
1. Set Up Vault Policies and Roles

• Create a Vault policy that grants read access to the secret paths your application will need. For example, suppose your secret is stored at secret/data/myapp/config; your policy (written in HCL) might look like this:

  # myapp-policy.hcl
  path "secret/data/myapp/config" {
   capabilities = ["read"]
  }

• Write the policy into Vault:
  vault policy write myapp-policy myapp-policy.hcl

• Next, configure a Kubernetes-auth role that binds a Kubernetes Service Account (or a set of them) to this policy. For instance:

  vault write auth/kubernetes/role/myapp-role \
   bound_service_account_names=myapp-serviceaccount \
   bound_service_account_namespaces=default \
   policies=myapp-policy \
   ttl=1h

This step makes sure that when a pod running under the specified service account authenticates (using a JWT from Kubernetes), Vault grants it a token that has the permissions in “myapp-policy.”

──────────────────────────────
2. Prepare Your Kubernetes Pod for Vault Agent Injection

The Vault Agent Injector works by scanning your pod manifests for Vault-related annotations. When proper annotations are found the injector automatically adds a sidecar container running the Vault Agent and mounts a shared volume into your application container.

Here’s an example pod manifest snippet:

  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  metadata:
   name: myapp-pod
   annotations:
    vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"
    vault.hashicorp.com/role: "myapp-role"
    # This annotation tells the agent which secret and key to read.
    vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-config: "secret/data/myapp/config"
    # Optionally, you can define a template to format the secret.
    vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-template-config: |
     {{- with secret "secret/data/myapp/config" -}}
     DB_PASSWORD={{ .Data.data.db_password }}
     {{- end }}
  spec:
   serviceAccountName: myapp-serviceaccount
   containers:
   - name: myapp
    image: myapp:latest
    volumeMounts:
    - name: vault-secret
     mountPath: /vault/secrets
   # You do not need to specify the vault-agent container;
   # it is injected automatically.
   volumes:
   - name: vault-secret
    emptyDir: {}

Key Points in the Manifest:

• The annotation vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject="true" signals that you want the Vault Agent to be injected.

• The vault.hashicorp.com/role annotation tells the agent which Vault role (and therefore which policies) to use when fetching secrets.

• The vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-<name> and vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-template-<name> annotations specify the secret path in Vault and (optional) a template for the file’s contents. In the above example, “config” is the name of the injected secret file that will be placed by default at /vault/secrets/config.

──────────────────────────────
3. How the Sidecar Injection Works

When the pod is created:

• The Vault Agent Injector (usually deployed as part of HashiCorp’s Vault Kubernetes integration) intercepts the pod creation.

• It reads the annotations, then automatically injects a Vault Agent sidecar container into the pod. This sidecar container authenticates with Vault (using the Kubernetes auth method) as the pod’s service account and retrieves the specified secrets.

• The Vault Agent writes these secrets into files on a shared volume. In our example, you’ll find the secrets at /vault/secrets/config within the pod’s file system.

──────────────────────────────
4. Reading the Secrets from the Application

Your application running in the main container can now read the secrets from the injected file (or files) on the shared volume. For instance, in your application code you could read the file stored at /vault/secrets/config.

• If you used a template to render the file (as shown above), your file might have contents like:
  DB_PASSWORD=supersecretpassword

• The application can read this file at startup or on demand to obtain the secret values (in this case, to use the DB_PASSWORD for connecting to a database).

──────────────────────────────
5. Security Considerations and Best Practices

• Ensure that only the necessary pods (using specific service accounts) can use the Vault role that has access to the required secrets.

• Limit the TTL and scope of tokens issued by Vault to reduce the potential impact of a compromised token.

• Monitor and audit access to Vault secrets.

• Consider setting up a sidecar that also handles secret renewals if your application runs long-lived processes.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

By using Vault’s sidecar injection, you eliminate the need to bake secrets into container images or pass them via environment variables at deployment time. Instead, the Vault Agent sidecar securely fetches secrets at pod startup, writes them to a shared volume (or injects them into environment variables in some configurations), and your application can simply read these files at runtime.

This pattern not only simplifies secret management but also improves security by ensuring that secret retrieval and renewal are handled centrally by Vault while maintaining a clear separation between application code and secret management.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
```

```python
# 假设 read_get_set() 已经按上述代码定义并且可以被直接调用。

    'criterion': ['gini', 'entropy']
}

best_score = -np.inf

for max_depth in param_grid['max_depth']:

        for min_samples_leaf in param_grid['min_samples_leaf']:
            for criterion in param_grid['criterion']:
                cv_scores = []
                for train_idx, val_idx in skf.split(X_train, y_train):
                    X_tr, X_val = X_train.iloc[train_idx], X_train.iloc[val_idx]
                    y_tr, y_val = y_train.iloc[train_idx], y_train.iloc[val_idx]
                    clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=max_depth,
                                                 min_samples_split=min_samples_split,
                                                 min_samples_leaf=min_samples_leaf,
                                                 criterion=criterion,
                                                 random_state=42)
                    clf.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
                    y_pred = clf.predict(X_val)
                    score = f1_score(y_val, y_pred)
                    cv_scores.append(score)
                avg_score = np.mean(cv_scores)

                if avg_score > best_score:
                    best_score = avg_score
                    best_params = (max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf, criterion)

# 用最佳参数训练最终模型
final_clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(
    max_depth=best_params[0],
    min_samples_split=best_params[1],
    min_samples_leaf=best_params[2],
    criterion=best_params[3],
    random_state=42
)
final_clf.fit(X_train, y_train)

# 预测测试集
test_pred = final_clf.predict(X_test)
```

#!/usr/bin/env python

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

def read_get_set():
    # 数据读取
    train_set = pd.read_csv('processed_data/train_features_label.csv')
    test_set = pd.read_csv('processed_data/test_features_label.csv')

    # 过滤掉 label 为 -1 的样本
    train_set = train_set[~train_set['label'].isin([-1])]
    test_set = test_set[~test_set['label'].isin([-1])]  # 如果测试集中也有-1值

    # 分割特征和标签

    y_train = train_set["label"]

    X_test = test_set.drop(["user_id", "merchant_id", "label"], axis=1, errors='ignore')
    return X_train, y_train, X_test, train_set, test_set

# 读取数据

# 定义参数网格
param_grid = {
    'max_depth': [None, 3, 5, 7, 10],
    'min_samples_split': [2, 5, 10]
}

# 设置交叉验证参数
n_splits = 5  # 5折交叉验证
kf = KFold(n_splits=n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

best_score = -np.inf  # 记录最高平均得分
best_params = {}

# 遍历参数组合
for max_depth in param_grid['max_depth']:
    for min_samples_split in param_grid['min_samples_split']:
        cv_scores = []  # 存储每折的分数

        # 手动交叉验证
        for train_index, val_index in kf.split(X_train):
            X_tr, X_val = X_train.iloc[train_index], X_train.iloc[val_index]
            y_tr, y_val = y_train.iloc[train_index], y_train.iloc[val_index]

            # 构造决策树模型（没有直接调用现成的调参 API）
            clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=max_depth, min_samples_split=min_samples_split, random_state=42)

            # 验证集预测并计算准确率
            y_pred = clf.predict(X_val)
            score = accuracy_score(y_val, y_pred)
            cv_scores.append(score)
        
        avg_score = np.mean(cv_scores)
        print("参数组合： max_depth={}， min_samples_split={}，平均准确率={:.4f}".format(max_depth, min_samples_split, avg_score))
        
        # 保存最高分及对应参数
        if avg_score > best_score:
            best_score = avg_score
            best_params = {
                'max_depth': max_depth,
                'min_samples_split': min_samples_split
            }

print("最佳参数：", best_params, "对应的平均准确率：", best_score)

# 使用最佳参数在整个训练集上训练最终模型
final_model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=best_params['max_depth'], 
                                     min_samples_split=best_params['min_samples_split'],

    # 如果需要将预测结果保存或后续评估，请继续编写代码
    print("测试集预测完成")

```c
#ifndef OS_CONSTRUCTOR_H

/* OS detection */
#if defined(__APPLE__)

    #define OS_WINDOWS 1
#elif defined(__unix__) || defined(__linux__)
    #define OS_UNIX 1
#else
    #error "Unknown or unsupported operating system"
#endif

/* CONSTRUCTOR definition */
#if defined(OS_WINDOWS)
    /* On Windows, use a CRT section trick for C89+MSVC/GCC/MinGW */
    #if defined(_MSC_VER)
        #pragma section(".CRT$XCU", read)
        #define CONSTRUCTOR(fn) \
            static void __cdecl fn(void); \
            __declspec(allocate(".CRT$XCU")) void (__cdecl* fn##_)(void) = fn; \
            static void __cdecl fn(void)
    #elif defined(__GNUC__)
        #define CONSTRUCTOR(fn) \
            static void fn(void); \
            static void (*fn##_)(void) __attribute__((section(".CRT$XCU"), used)) = fn; \
            static void fn(void)
    #else
        #error "Windows compiler not supported for CONSTRUCTOR macro"
    #endif
#else
    /* On UNIX (and MacOS), use constructor attribute */
    #define CONSTRUCTOR(fn) \
        static void fn(void) __attribute__((constructor)); \
        static void fn(void)
```

```rust
use std::os::unix::io::AsRawFd;
use std::io;
use std::time::Duration;
use std::net::Socket;

pub trait SockOpt {
    fn read_timeout(&self) -> io::Result<Option<Duration>>;
    fn set_read_timeout(&self, duration: Option<Duration>) -> io::Result<()>;
}

impl SockOpt for tokio::net::UdpSocket {
    fn read_timeout(&self) -> io::Result<Option<Duration>> {
        let fd = self.as_raw_fd();
        // 创建临时的 Socket 实例
        let sock = unsafe { Socket::from_raw_fd(fd) };

        let timeout = sock.read_timeout()?;
        // 转移所有权，避免关闭文件描述符
        let _ = sock.into_raw_fd();
        Ok(timeout)
    }

    fn set_read_timeout(&self, duration: Option<Duration>) -> io::Result<()> {
        let fd = self.as_raw_fd();
        // 创建临时的 Socket 实例
        let sock = unsafe { Socket::from_raw_fd(fd) };
        // 执行设置操作
        let res = sock.set_read_timeout(duration);
        // 转移所有权，避免关闭文件描述符
        let _ = sock.into_raw_fd();
        res
    }
}
```

```rust
impl SockOpt for tokio::net::UdpSocket {
    fn set_read_timeout(&self, duration: Option<Duration>) -> io::Result<()> {
        let fd = self.as_raw_fd();
```

```rust
use std::os::unix::io::AsRawFd;
use std::io;
use std::time::Duration;
use std::net::Socket;

pub trait SockOpt {
    fn read_timeout(&self) -> io::Result<Option<Duration>>;
    fn set_read_timeout(&self, duration: Option<Duration>) -> io::Result<()>;
}

impl SockOpt for tokio::net::UdpSocket {
    fn read_timeout(&self) -> io::Result<Option<Duration>> {

        let _ = sock.into_raw_fd();

    }
```

```rust
impl SockOpt for tokio::net::UdpSocket {
    fn set_read_timeout(&self, duration: Option<Duration>) -> io::Result<()> {
        let fd = self.as_raw_fd();
        let timeout = duration.map(|d| {
            timeval {

}
```

```go
	"sync"
```

```go
			for j := 0; j < appendsPerGoroutine; j++ {

			}
		}()
	}

	// Wait for all goroutines to finish
	wg.Wait()

	// Calculate expected vs actual results
	expected := totalGoroutines * appendsPerGoroutine
	actual := len(s)
	fmt.Printf("Expected: %d, Actual: %d\n", expected, actual)
```

1. **Shared Slice**: The slice `s` is a global variable shared by all goroutines.
2. **Concurrent Appends**: Each goroutine appends `1` to the slice `appendsPerGoroutine` times.
3. **Race Condition**: Since appends are not atomic:
   - Multiple goroutines may read the slice's length and capacity simultaneously.
   - If the slice needs resizing (due to insufficient capacity), multiple goroutines might attempt to reallocate the underlying array concurrently, leading to lost writes.

   ```
     main.main()
     ...

     main.main()
     ...
   ...
   ```

## My Answer

The user wants to change their code so that when browsing for a folder, the file dialog shows the files inside the folder (i.e., displays the folder's content for selection), but the end result is that their program selects/works with the folder (not an individual file).

**Problem Context**:  
`filedialog.askdirectory()` selects a folder, but does not browse into and show the files inside it.  
`filedialog.askopenfilename(s)` (or `askopenfilenames`) shows files, but returns files (not a folder/directory).

**Common solution in tkinter**:  
Since tkinter's `askdirectory()` doesn't preview files inside the folder, but `askopenfilenames()` does, a common workaround is to open a file dialog (using `askopenfilenames` or `askopenfilename`), let the user see files (and optionally select one), and then extract the folder from the selected file(s). You then list all files in that folder as before. This ensures the user can see and browse the folder's content, but your app still operates at the folder level.

### Example solution

Replace your `open_directory` with:

```python
def open_directory(self):
    file_paths = filedialog.askopenfilenames(
        title="Select a file from the target folder",
        filetypes=[("Image files", "*.png;*.jpg;*.jpeg;*.gif;*.bmp;*.webp"),
                   ("All files", "*.*")]
    )
    if file_paths:
        directory = os.path.dirname(file_paths[0])
        self.image_list = sorted([
            os.path.join(directory, f)
            for f in os.listdir(directory)
            if f.lower().endswith(('png', 'jpg', 'jpeg', 'gif', 'bmp', 'webp'))
        ], key=lambda x: os.path.basename(x).lower())

        if not self.image_list:
            messagebox.showerror("Error", "No images found in this folder.")
            return
        self.image_index = 0
        self.update_image_listbox()
        self.show_image()
        self.image_listbox.focus_set()
```

*Optionally add a label somewhere in the UI to show the current folder's name.*

### Notes:

- This pattern is well-accepted for tkinter because the toolkit doesn't have a directory dialog that lists files.
- If you need to allow users to select only folders (not files), you must accept the limitation that `askdirectory` does not show file lists.
- You can show the selected directory path somewhere in your GUI for clarity.

def update_tags_for_image(self, filename):
    # Clear all checkboxes
    for category in self.tag_vars:
        for var in self.tag_vars[category].values():
            var.set(0)
    
    # Clear current tags
    self.tags = {}
    
    # Set tags based on filename
    name_parts = os.path.splitext(filename)[0].split('_')
    name_parts = [part for part in name_parts if not part.isdigit()]
    
    first_category = list(self.tag_options.keys())[0]
    
    # Handle type-to-match category
    for part in name_parts:
        if part.lower() in [option.lower() for option in self.tag_options[first_category]]:
            self.tags[first_category] = [part]
            self.type_to_match_var.set(part)
            break
    
    # Handle other categories
    for part in name_parts:
        for category, options in list(self.tag_options.items())[1:]:
            if part.lower() in [option.lower() for option in options]:
                self.tag_vars[category][part].set(1)
                if category not in self.tags:
                    self.tags[category] = []
                if part not in self.tags[category]:
                    self.tags[category].append(part)

    # Store tags for this image
    self.image_tags[filename] = self.tags.copy()

    self.update_new_filename_label()

def update_new_filename_label(self):

    tags = []
    for category in self.tag_options.keys():
        if category in self.tags:
            # Sort the tags for this category alphabetically
            category_tags = sorted(self.tags[category])
            tags.extend(category_tags)
    
    if tags:
        new_filename = "_".join(tags).lower() + ".webp"
        self.current_tags_label.config(text=f"New Filename: {new_filename}")
    else:
        self.current_tags_label.config(text="New Filename: No tags selected")

        if category in self.tags:

            category_tags = sorted(self.tags[category])

    if not tags:

        return

def resize_current_image(self):

        return

    frame_width = self.image_frame.winfo_width()
    frame_height = self.image_frame.winfo_height()

    if frame_width <= 1 or frame_height <= 1:  # Frame not properly sized yet
        self.root.update_idletasks()
        frame_width = self.image_frame.winfo_width()
        frame_height = self.image_frame.winfo_height()

    img_width, img_height = self.current_image.size
    aspect_ratio = img_width / img_height

    if frame_width / frame_height > aspect_ratio:
        new_height = frame_height
        new_width = int(new_height * aspect_ratio)
    else:
        new_width = frame_width
        new_height = int(new_width / aspect_ratio)

    resized_image = self.current_image.copy()
    resized_image.thumbnail((new_width, new_height), Image.LANCZOS)

    # Add a white border to the image
    bordered_image = Image.new("RGB", (new_width + 2, new_height + 2), color="white")
    bordered_image.paste(resized_image, (1, 1))

    self.image_label.config(image=photo)
    self.image_label.image = photo  # Keep a reference

Let's break down the user's request, possible interpretations, and the ideal solution.

## User Request Analysis

The user wants to **change how the folder selection works** in a tkinter app. They want that, when they browse for a folder to open (using the "Open Directory" action), 
- The dialog **shows the contents (files) of that folder** during selection,
- But in the app itself, the **selected folder is still what's acted upon** (its image files are shown/listed/processed).

**Problem:**  
tkinter's `askdirectory()` - standard folder dialog - doesn't show files, just folders.  
tkinter's `askopenfilename()` / `askopenfilenames()` shows files (in a folder), but returns a file path, not a folder.

So the user is asking how to, when opening ("Open Directory"), allow browsing into a folder *and seeing its contents* **before confirming**, but *still select the folder* as the unit to be worked on.

## My Ideal Answer

### Explanation

There is *no native* tkinter dialog that shows the files *inside* a folder and returns the folder path.  
- `askdirectory()` is a pure directory browser (shows only folders, not files).
- `askopenfilename()` or `askopenfilenames()` can show files, but they return file paths, not folder.

**Workaround:**  
- Use `askopenfilename()` or `askopenfilenames()` and let the user pick a file in the desired folder. Then your code can use `os.path.dirname(file_path)` to get the folder, and list **all images** in that folder as you do in your code.  
- This way, the dialog shows files as requested, and your code still works on the folder.

### How to modify code

Replace the `askdirectory()` call in your `open_directory` method:

```python
def open_directory(self):
    file_paths = filedialog.askopenfilenames(
        title="Select an image from the folder",
        filetypes=[("Image files", "*.png;*.jpg;*.jpeg;*.gif;*.bmp;*.webp"),
                   ("All files", "*.*")]
    )
    if file_paths:
        directory = os.path.dirname(file_paths[0])
        self.image_list = sorted(
            [os.path.join(directory, f)
             for f in os.listdir(directory)
             if f.lower().endswith(('png', 'jpg', 'jpeg', 'gif', 'bmp', 'webp'))],
            key=lambda x: os.path.basename(x).lower()
        )
        if not self.image_list:
            messagebox.showerror("Error", "No images found in the selected folder.")
            return
        self.image_index = 0
        self.update_image_listbox()
        self.show_image()
        self.image_listbox.focus_set()
```
- The user will see the files (and can select one or more).
- Internally, you use the folder containing the first file (or only one file if using `askopenfilename()`).
- If the user cancels, do nothing.
- You still process the whole folder's image files, as before.

### Optional: show the selected directory in the GUI

Optionally, you can add a Label to your UI (top frame) showing the currently selected folder, to make it clear to the user which folder is in use.

### Note

- This is a *common and accepted hack* for when you want to show files but select a folder in tkinter.
- If you want the user to be able to select subfolders too (not just those with images), you could let the user choose either a folder (askdirectory) or an image file (askopenfilename) with a menu option, but that is more complex.

## Evaluation

Now let's compare the assistants' answers to my solution:

### Assistant A

- **What does it suggest?**
    - Adds a Label to the UI to show the currently-selected folder after selection.
    - Leaves selection as `askdirectory()` - pure folder selection.

    - But this just *displays* the path you picked in the UI.
    - The open dialog is unchanged: it is still just a directory browser; files aren't shown in the dialog during selection.

- **How helpful/relevant is this?**
    - It adds a UI feature, but does **not address the actual problem**: the user wants the dialog they use to choose the folder to *show files inside the folder* before they pick it.
    - The assistant helps make things clearer in the UI *after* selecting, but does not change the selection experience as the user requests.

- **Other notes:**

### Assistant B

- A does not address the root issue (problem with the dialog, not post-selection UI feedback).

def show_image(self):
    if self.image_list:
        image_path = self.image_list[self.image_index]
        filename = os.path.basename(image_path)     
        try:
            self.current_image = Image.open(image_path)
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Debug: Error opening image: {e}")
            return  # Exit the method if we can't open the image
        
        self.resize_current_image()
        
        self.current_image_label.config(text=f"Current Image: {filename}")
        
        # Clear all existing tags and checkboxes
        self.clear_all_tags()

        # Load or update tags for this image
        self.update_tags_for_image(filename)
        
        # Update type-to-match
        first_category = list(self.tag_options.keys())[0]
        if first_category in self.tags and self.tags[first_category]:
            self.type_to_match_var.set(self.tags[first_category][0])
            # Select the item in the listbox
            items = self.type_to_match_listbox.get(0, END)
            if self.tags[first_category][0] in items:
                index = items.index(self.tags[first_category][0])
                self.type_to_match_listbox.selection_clear(0, END)
                self.type_to_match_listbox.selection_set(index)
                self.type_to_match_listbox.see(index)
        else:
            self.type_to_match_var.set("")
            self.type_to_match_listbox.selection_clear(0, END)

        # Update checkboxes
        for category, tags in self.tags.items():
            if category in self.tag_vars:
                for option in self.tag_vars[category]:
                    if option in tags:
                        self.tag_vars[category][option].set(1)
                    else:
                        self.tag_vars[category][option].set(0)
        
        self.update_new_filename_label()
        
        # Force update of the UI
        self.root.update_idletasks()
    else:
        print("Debug: No images in the list")

def update_tags_for_image(self, filename):
    # Clear all checkboxes
    for category in self.tag_vars:
        for var in self.tag_vars[category].values():
            var.set(0)
    
    # Clear current tags
    self.tags = {}
    
    # Set tags based on filename
    name_parts = os.path.splitext(filename)[0].split('_')
    name_parts = [part for part in name_parts if not part.isdigit()]
    
    first_category = list(self.tag_options.keys())[0]
    
    # Handle type-to-match category
    for part in name_parts:
        if part.lower() in [option.lower() for option in self.tag_options[first_category]]:
            self.tags[first_category] = [part]
            self.type_to_match_var.set(part)
            break
    
    # Handle other categories
    for part in name_parts:
        for category, options in list(self.tag_options.items())[1:]:
            if part.lower() in [option.lower() for option in options]:
                self.tag_vars[category][part].set(1)
                if category not in self.tags:
                    self.tags[category] = []
                if part not in self.tags[category]:
                    self.tags[category].append(part)

    # Store tags for this image
    self.image_tags[filename] = self.tags.copy()

    self.update_new_filename_label()

def update_new_filename_label(self):
    if not self.image_list:
        self.current_tags_label.config(text="New Filename: No image selected")
        return

    tags = []
    for category in self.tag_options.keys():
        if category in self.tags:
            # Sort the tags for this category alphabetically
            category_tags = sorted(self.tags[category])
            tags.extend(category_tags)
    
    if tags:
        new_filename = "_".join(tags).lower() + ".webp"
        self.current_tags_label.config(text=f"New Filename: {new_filename}")
    else:
        self.current_tags_label.config(text="New Filename: No tags selected")

def rename_image(self):
    if not self.image_list:
        messagebox.showerror("Error", "No images to rename.")
        return
    
    tags = []
    for category in self.tag_options.keys():
        if category in self.tags:
            # Sort the tags for this category alphabetically
            category_tags = sorted(self.tags[category])
            tags.extend(category_tags)

    if not tags:
        messagebox.showerror("Error", "At least one tag is required.")
        return

    directory = os.path.dirname(self.image_list[self.image_index])
    base_name = "_".join(tags).lower()  # Convert base name to lowercase
    new_name = f"{base_name}.webp"
    new_path = os.path.join(directory, new_name)

    i = 1
    while os.path.exists(new_path):
        new_name = f"{base_name}_{i:03d}.webp"
        new_path = os.path.join(directory, new_name)
        i += 1

    # Convert and save the image as a WebP file
    image = Image.open(self.image_list[self.image_index])
    image.save(new_path, format='WEBP')

    old_path = self.image_list[self.image_index]
    os.remove(old_path)
    self.image_list[self.image_index] = new_path

    self.tags.clear()
    self.update_new_filename_label()
    for category in self.tag_vars:
        for var in self.tag_vars[category].values():
            var.set(False)
    self.update_image_list(os.path.dirname(new_path))
    
    # Select and load the newly renamed image
    new_index = self.image_list.index(new_path)
    self.image_index = new_index
    self.image_listbox.select_clear(0, END)
    self.image_listbox.select_set(new_index)
    self.image_listbox.see(new_index)
    self.show_image()

def resize_current_image(self):
    if not hasattr(self, 'current_image'):
        return

    frame_width = self.image_frame.winfo_width()
    frame_height = self.image_frame.winfo_height()

    if frame_width <= 1 or frame_height <= 1:  # Frame not properly sized yet
        self.root.update_idletasks()
        frame_width = self.image_frame.winfo_width()
        frame_height = self.image_frame.winfo_height()

    img_width, img_height = self.current_image.size
    aspect_ratio = img_width / img_height

    if frame_width / frame_height > aspect_ratio:
        new_height = frame_height
        new_width = int(new_height * aspect_ratio)
    else:
        new_width = frame_width
        new_height = int(new_width / aspect_ratio)

    resized_image = self.current_image.copy()
    resized_image.thumbnail((new_width, new_height), Image.LANCZOS)

    # Add a white border to the image
    bordered_image = Image.new("RGB", (new_width + 2, new_height + 2), color="white")
    bordered_image.paste(resized_image, (1, 1))

    photo = ImageTk.PhotoImage(bordered_image)
    self.image_label.config(image=photo)
    self.image_label.image = photo  # Keep a reference

def update_tags(self, category, option):
    is_checked = self.tag_vars[category][option].get()
    
    if category not in self.tags:
        self.tags[category] = []
    
    # Only clear other selections for the first category (type-to-match)
    if category == list(self.tag_options.keys())[0]:
        for other_option in self.tag_vars[category]:
            if other_option != option:
                self.tag_vars[category][other_option].set(0)
        self.tags[category] = []  # Clear previous selections
    
    if is_checked and option not in self.tags[category]:
        self.tags[category].append(option)
    elif not is_checked and option in self.tags[category]:
        self.tags[category].remove(option)
    
    if not self.tags[category]:
        del self.tags[category]
    
    # Update tags for the current image
    current_image = os.path.basename(self.image_list[self.image_index])
    self.image_tags[current_image] = self.tags.copy()

```python
import pandas as pd
```
```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from transitions import Machine
import sys
```

    # Define the states that represent each analysis step.
    states = ['idle', 'loading', 'preprocessing', 'analyzing', 'visualizing', 'generating_report', 'finished']

    def on_analyze(self):

        print("[ANALYZING] Performing analysis...")
        # Compute publication trends per year.
        publications_per_year = self.bibliometrics.groupby('Year').size()
        # Compute total citations per year.
        citations_per_year = self.bibliometrics.groupby('Year')['Citations'].sum()
        # Determine top 10 authors.

        ax[1].set_ylabel("Total Citations")

        # Plot top authors: Horizontal bar chart.

        ax[2].set_title("Top 10 Authors")
        ax[2].set_xlabel("Number of Publications")

        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()

    def on_generate_report(self):
        """Automatically generate a textual report summarizing the insights (auto-gen report)."""
        print("[REPORT] Generating the bibliometric analysis report...")
        report_text = []
        report_text.append("Bibliometric Analysis Report")

        report_text.append(self.insights['citations_per_year'].to_string())

    def on_finish(self):

def main():

Below is an example Python script that implements a state‐driven “stateflow” approach to load, preprocess, analyze, and visualize bibliometric data from a CSV file. In this example, we use the transitions library to create a state machine that “flows” through the stages of the analysis. In the analysis stage the script computes publication trends and rankings of top authors. In the “autogen” (automatic generation) stage the script automatically produces a textual report with the insights.

Before running the script be sure to install the required packages:
  • transitions (for the state machine)
  • pandas
  • matplotlib

  pip install transitions pandas matplotlib

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
A bibliometric analyzer that uses a stateflow approach to automatically generate insights.
It loads bibliometric data (e.g., research paper records with publication year,
citations, authors, etc.) from a CSV file, preprocesses it, analyzes publication trends,
plots the results, and then auto-generates a textual report.
"""

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from transitions import Machine
import sys

class BibliometricAnalyzer:
    # Define the states that represent each analysis step.
    states = ['idle', 'loading', 'preprocessing', 'analyzing', 'visualizing', 'generating_report', 'finished']

    def __init__(self, data_path):
        self.data_path = data_path                # CSV file path containing bibliometrics
        self.bibliometrics = None                 # Pandas DataFrame for the data
        self.insights = {}                        # Dictionary to store analysis results and insights

        # Setup the state machine using the transitions library.
        self.machine = Machine(model=self, states=BibliometricAnalyzer.states, initial='idle')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='load_data', source='idle', dest='loading', before='on_load')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='preprocess_data', source='loading', dest='preprocessing', before='on_preprocess')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='analyze', source='preprocessing', dest='analyzing', before='on_analyze')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='visualize', source='analyzing', dest='visualizing', before='on_visualize')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='generate_report', source='visualizing', dest='generating_report', before='on_generate_report')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='finish', source='generating_report', dest='finished', before='on_finish')

    def on_load(self):
        """Load bibliometric data from the CSV file."""
        try:
            self.bibliometrics = pd.read_csv(self.data_path)
            print(f"[LOADING] Data loaded successfully with {len(self.bibliometrics)} records.")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[ERROR] Failed to load data: {e}")
            sys.exit(1)

    def on_preprocess(self):
        """Preprocess the data: drop missing values and ensure correct types."""
        initial_count = len(self.bibliometrics)
        self.bibliometrics.dropna(inplace=True)
        try:
            # Ensure 'Year' is an integer and 'Citations' is numeric.
            self.bibliometrics['Year'] = self.bibliometrics['Year'].astype(int)
            self.bibliometrics['Citations'] = pd.to_numeric(self.bibliometrics['Citations'])
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[ERROR] Failed during type conversion: {e}")
            sys.exit(1)
        print(f"[PREPROCESS] Data cleaned: removed {initial_count - len(self.bibliometrics)} incomplete records.")

    def on_analyze(self):
        """Analyze the bibliometric data and auto-generate insights."""
        print("[ANALYZING] Performing analysis...")
        # Compute publication trends per year.
        publications_per_year = self.bibliometrics.groupby('Year').size()
        # Compute total citations per year.
        citations_per_year = self.bibliometrics.groupby('Year')['Citations'].sum()
        # Determine top 10 authors.
        # Assume the CSV has an 'Authors' column with authors separated by commas.
        authors_series = self.bibliometrics['Authors'].str.split(',')
        authors_exploded = authors_series.explode().str.strip()
        top_authors = authors_exploded.value_counts().head(10)

        self.insights['publications_per_year'] = publications_per_year
        self.insights['citations_per_year'] = citations_per_year
        self.insights['top_authors'] = top_authors

        # Print out key insight summaries.
        print("[ANALYZING] Publication trends by year:")
        print(publications_per_year)
        print("[ANALYZING] Top 10 authors:")
        print(top_authors)

    def on_visualize(self):
        """Visualize the insights using Matplotlib."""
        print("[VISUALIZING] Generating plots...")
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))

        # Plot publications per year: Bar chart.
        self.insights['publications_per_year'].plot(kind='bar', ax=ax[0])
        ax[0].set_title("Publications Per Year")
        ax[0].set_xlabel("Year")
        ax[0].set_ylabel("Number of Publications")

        # Plot citations per year: Line plot.
        self.insights['citations_per_year'].plot(kind='line', marker='o', ax=ax[1])
        ax[1].set_title("Total Citations Per Year")
        ax[1].set_xlabel("Year")
        ax[1].set_ylabel("Total Citations")

        # Plot top authors: Horizontal bar chart.
        self.insights['top_authors'].plot(kind='barh', ax=ax[2])
        ax[2].set_title("Top 10 Authors")
        ax[2].set_xlabel("Number of Publications")

        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()

    def on_generate_report(self):
        """Automatically generate a textual report summarizing the insights (auto-gen report)."""
        print("[REPORT] Generating the bibliometric analysis report...")
        report_text = []
        report_text.append("Bibliometric Analysis Report")
        report_text.append("============================\n")
        report_text.append("1. Publication Trend by Year:")
        report_text.append(self.insights['publications_per_year'].to_string())
        report_text.append("\n2. Total Citations Per Year:")
        report_text.append(self.insights['citations_per_year'].to_string())
        report_text.append("\n3. Top 10 Authors:")
        report_text.append(self.insights['top_authors'].to_string())
        report_text = "\n".join(report_text)

        try:
            with open('bibliometric_report.txt', 'w') as f:
                f.write(report_text)
            print("[REPORT] Report successfully generated as 'bibliometric_report.txt'.")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[ERROR] Failed to write report: {e}")

    def on_finish(self):
        """Cleanup or final logging."""
        print("[FINISHED] Bibliometric analysis workflow is complete.")

def main():
    # Check for CSV file path argument.
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print("Usage: python bibliometric_analyzer.py <path_to_csv_file>")
        sys.exit(1)

    data_path = sys.argv[1]

    # Instantiate the analyzer.
    analyzer = BibliometricAnalyzer(data_path)

    # Execute the stateflow: the transitions will automatically call the before callbacks.
    analyzer.load_data()         # Transitions from 'idle' to 'loading'
    analyzer.preprocess_data()   # 'loading' -> 'preprocessing'
    analyzer.analyze()           # 'preprocessing' -> 'analyzing'
    analyzer.visualize()         # 'analyzing' -> 'visualizing'
    analyzer.generate_report()   # 'visualizing' -> 'generating_report'
    analyzer.finish()            # 'generating_report' -> 'finished'

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation:

1. The BibliometricAnalyzer class defines a series of states from idle, loading, preprocessing, analyzing, visualizing, generating_report, and finished.
2. Each state transition is triggered via a method (e.g., load_data, preprocess_data, etc.). The “before” callbacks (e.g., on_load, on_preprocess, …) implement the functionality.
3. In the analysis stage, the script automatically computes:
    • The number of publications per year.
    • The total number of citations per year.
    • The top 10 authors (assuming the “Authors” column contains comma‐separated names).
4. The visualization stage uses Matplotlib to plot the insights.
5. Finally, the report stage “autogen” creates a text report with the key findings.

To run this script:
  1. Save it as bibliometric_analyzer.py.
  2. Prepare a CSV file (say, research_bibliometrics.csv) with at least the columns: Year, Citations, Authors, etc.
  3. Run:
     python bibliometric_analyzer.py research_bibliometrics.csv

This script is a template that you can extend further—for example, including additional states, more advanced network analyses (e.g., using NetworkX for collaboration networks), or interactive dashboards.

Let's break down and answer the problem first, then compare the provided AI answers.

## My Analysis & Solution

**What the code attempts to do:**  
- For S (up to 10) stores, treat it as a TSP over (S+1) nodes, the "key intersections" (stores + home).
- Build an all-pairs distance matrix between these nodes using Dijkstra from each node.
- For each permutation of store visit order, compute the route (start at 0, visit all stores in some order, return to 0), minimize total route length.
  
**Major potential reasons for WA:**
1. **Not sorting the stops before next_permutation**: If the vector is not sorted, next_permutation will NOT enumerate all permutations.
2. **Graph edge handling:** If multiple roads exist between the same two intersections, only the last read is stored, not the minimum value. This can lead to longer-than-minimum paths.
3. **Integer overflow:** Using `int` instead of `long long` could overflow, especially if distances are large.
4. **Minor code issues**:
   - Popping the last element (with `pop_back`) after building the distances, which could be error-prone if "0" is used in other calculations.
   - No explicit check or exception handling for negative weights in Dijkstra (but the problem probably disallows negative lengths).

**Test:**
First, the not-sorted permutation is the most likely culprit, but both (1) and (2) above are genuine code bugs that could result in WA.

## Assistant A
- Correctly identifies the **lack of sort before next_permutation**, explaining clearly with an example why this causes missing permutations.
- Also notes the possible integer overflow risk due to use of `int` instead of `long long`.
- Does **not mention** the possible error with multiple edges (higher or lower D values on repeated roads)—which is possible in the input and not handled in original code.

## Assistant B
- Points out the **need to always take the minimum D for a pair** when multiple roads exist, and provides code that explicitly implements this.
- Describes and fixes permutation and integer type handling.
- Supplies a full working solution with all code changes.
- However, the permutation part is not directly commented on; but the code provided constructs the order vector and uses next_permutation, implying correctly that it starts with ordered permutation.

## Summary
- **Assistant A**: Focuses on the permutation oversight, which is the *most common reason* for WA here. Concise, focused, and correct—but misses the possible bug with multiple roads between the same nodes.
- **Assistant B**: Focuses on multiple edges bug, provides a full alternative implementation, addresses edge case, properly uses Dijkstra and permutation, and seems to no longer assume edges are replaced rather than minimized—which is a possible source of WA.

## Verdict and Missing Info
- **Neither assistant asked for a failing test case or the judge's feedback, but that's not necessary here due to clear root causes and concise prompt.**
- **Assistant A omits mention of the multiple-edges issue, which *can* cause WA if the test set includes such cases.**
- **Assistant B gives a full new code, which may be slightly excessive, but their explanation is correct, and they explicitly mention the multiple-edges issue, which the user’s code is indeed vulnerable to.**
- **Assistant B implicitly covers the permutation issue by building the order vector and permuting it from sorted order.**
- **Assistant B uses long long, avoids overflow.**

Thus, **Assistant B's answer is slightly more complete with respect to possible causes and how to avoid WA in all cases**, even if it is a bit more verbose.

---

**My final verdict is: [[B>A]]**

#include <bits/extc++.h>
#include "custom_algorithms.hpp"

using namespace __gnu_pbds;
using namespace std;

using namespace custom_algorithms;

using ll = long long int;
using ull = unsigned long long int;

using pll = pair<ll, ll>;

void solve(void);

int main(void) {
        ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false);
        cin.tie(nullptr);
        cout.tie(nullptr);

        int T;
        cin >> T;

        for (int i=0; i<T; i++) {
                solve();
        }
        
        return 0;
}

void solve(void) {
        int N, M;
        cin >> N >> M;

        gp_hash_table<int, gp_hash_table<int, int>> graph;
        
        for (int i=0; i<M; i++) {
                int X, Y, D;
                cin >> X >> Y >> D;
                
                graph[X][Y] = D;
                graph[Y][X] = D;
        }

        int S;
        cin >> S;

        vector<int> stopovers(S+1);
        stopovers[S] = 0;
        
        for (int i=0; i<S; i++) {
                cin >> stopovers[i];
        }
        
        gp_hash_table<int, gp_hash_table<int, int>> shortestPath;
                
        for (auto& start : stopovers) {
                gp_hash_table<int, int> temp = shortest_path::dijkstra::getShortestPath(graph, start);
                
                for (auto& stopover : stopovers) {
                        shortestPath[start][stopover] = temp[stopover];
                }
        }

        stopovers.pop_back();

        int minimum = INT_MAX;
        
        do {
                int curr = 0;
                int candidate = 0;
                
                for (auto& stopover : stopovers) {
                        candidate += shortestPath[curr][stopover];
                        curr = stopover;
                }
                candidate += shortestPath[curr][0];
                
                minimum = min(minimum, candidate);
        } while (next_permutation(stopovers.begin(), stopovers.end()));

        cout << minimum << '\n';
}

    namespace fft {
        long double const_pi(void) {
            return std::atan(1) * 4;
        }

        void FFT(std::vector<std::complex<long double>>& a, const std::complex<long double>& w) {
            size_t n = a.size();

            if (n == 1) {
                return;
            }

            std::vector<std::complex<long double>> a_even(n/2), a_odd(n/2);

            for (size_t i=0; i<(n/2); i++) {
                a_even[i] = a[2 * i];
                a_odd[i] = a[2 * i + 1];
            }

            std::complex<long double> w_squared = w * w;

            FFT(a_even, w_squared);
            FFT(a_odd, w_squared);

            std::complex<long double> w_i = 1;

            for (size_t i=0; i<(n/2); i++) {
                a[i] = a_even[i] + w_i * a_odd[i];
                a[i + (n/2)] = a_even[i] - w_i * a_odd[i];

                w_i *= w;
            }
        }

        std::vector<std::complex<long double>> convolution(std::vector<std::complex<long double>> a, std::vector<std::complex<long double>> b, bool getIntegerResult = false) {
            size_t n = 1;
            long double pi = const_pi();

            while (n <= a.size() || n <= b.size()) {
                n <<= 1;
            }
            n <<= 1;

            a.resize(n);
            b.resize(n);

            std::vector<std::complex<long double>> c(n);

            std::complex<long double> w(cos(2 * pi / n), sin(2 * pi / n));

            FFT(a, w);
            FFT(b, w);

            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                c[i] = a[i] * b[i];
            }

            FFT(c, std::complex<long double>(w.real(), -w.imag()));

            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                c[i] /= std::complex<long double>(n, 0);
                if (getIntegerResult) {
                    c[i] = std::complex<long double>(round(c[i].real()), round(c[i].imag()));

First, I’ll generate my own answer to the prompt.

---

**My Answer:**

The user is asking how perceptual 2D color opponent axes (like R-G, B-(R+G)/2) relate to a more mathematical, symmetric 3D set of differences (like R-(G+B), G-(R+B), B-(R+G)), especially in the context of “infinite saturation compression”: taking color to extremes along these axes.

Let’s clarify the spaces:

- **Perceptual (2D opponent):**
  - \( a \sim R - G \) ("red–green" axis)
  - \( b \sim B - \frac{R+G}{2} \) ("blue–yellow" axis)

- **Mathematical symmetric (3D):**
  - \( a' = R - (G+B) \)
  - \( b' = G - (R+B) \)
  - \( c' = B - (R+G) \)

But these three differences are not independent, because \( a'+b'+c' = 0 \) (sum to zero). This means they effectively span a 2D plane, like the opponent axes.

**Mapping from 3D to 2D:**

You can write the opponent axes as linear combinations (projections) of the symmetric differences. For example:

- \( a = R - G = [R-(G+B)] - [G-(R+B)] / 2 = (a' - b') / 2 \)
- \( b = B - \frac{R+G}{2} = [B-(R+G)] / 2 = c'/2 \)

Thus:
- Perceptual "red–green" = \( (a' - b')/2 \)
- Perceptual "blue–yellow" = \( c'/2 \)

**Mapping from 2D back to 3D:**

If you have (a, b), can you get a corresponding (a', b', c')? There's not a unique mapping since you're going from 2D to 3D, but a canonical way is to “embed” (a, b) into the 2D plane in 3D, for example by choosing b' = 0:

- \( a' = 2a \)
- \( b' = 0 \)
- \( c' = 2b \)

Or, more generally, for any (a, b), you can reconstruct a triplet (a', b', c') up to an additive constant (since the sum must be zero).

**Infinite saturation compression:**

In “infinite saturation” (maximally saturated colors), this corresponds to moving away from the origin in the 2D plane. In the 3D symmetric difference model, this means moving out along the plane \( a'+b'+c' = 0 \) in the direction associated with (a,b) as projected back to (a',b',c').

**Summary:**

- The 3D symmetric difference coordinates can be linearly projected onto the perceptual 2D axes.

The a', b', c' system is “symmetric” and additive: a' + b' + c' = 0 for all R,G,B. This is because:  
a' + b' + c' = [R-(G+B)] + [G-(R+B)] + [B-(R+G)] = (R+G+B) - 2(R+G+B) = -(R+G+B)

But since it appears a', b', c' serve only as chromatic axes (with luminance factored out), their sum is always negative the total brightness, and only two are independent.

---

**Step 2: Relating the spaces**  
Let’s relate the “symmetric” a', b', c' axes to the “perceptual” a, b axes:

- a = R - G  
- b = B - (R+G)/2

Let’s express these in terms of a', b', c':

a' = R - (G + B)  
b' = G - (R + B)  
c' = B - (R + G)

a' - b' = R - (G+B) - [G - (R+B)] = R - G - B - G + R + B = 2(R-G).  
So (a'-b')/2 = R-G = a.

Similarly, c' = B - (R+G) = 2*[B - (R+G)/2] = 2b.

Thus, the 2D perceptual “opponent” axes are just:
- a = (a' - b')/2 = R-G  
- b = c'/2 = B - (R+G)/2

So, the mapping from the 3D “symmetric” space to the 2D perceptual space is a linear projection:
- (a', b', c') → (a, b) = ((a'-b')/2, c'/2)

At infinite saturation, you would be considering colors whose chromatic content is maximized (distance from the origin in chromatic space is very large, usually with luminance constrained, e.g., all possible “pure” chromaticities).

- Perceptual chromatic vector = [((a'-b')/2), (c'/2)]

- a' = a  
- b' = -a  
- c' = 2b

The symmetric 3D system contains redundant (dependent) information; only two opponent (perceptual) axes are independent. To get perceptual opponent channels and the correct chromatic sense even at infinite saturation, you project the symmetric 3D vector onto the two perceptually-relevant axes:  
- Red-Green = (a'-b')/2  
- Blue-Yellow = c'/2

The paper’s findings about evolving foreign direct investment (FDI) networks offer crucial guidance for policymakers, businesses, and stakeholders seeking to maximize the benefits of global investment flows while minimizing associated risks.

They should develop sector-targeted strategies, especially in industries where centralization is easing, as these present better opportunities for new entrants. Fostering absorptive capacity and local technological know-how will also help less central countries attract higher-quality foreign investment, while regional collaboration and integration can create larger markets that are more appealing to investors.

At the industry level, the contrasting network structures highlight the need for nuanced strategies. Where FDI networks are becoming less centralized, countries can position themselves by cultivating competitive advantages or niche specializations, allowing them to attract investment.  – Indirect saving: 2 days × $1,000 = $2,000.
 – Net saving = $2,000 − $1,480 = $520.
 – Thus, fast tracking between J and K yields a marginal benefit.

• Crashing was considered on activities with heavy machinery involvement and long durations; however, in our calculations the extra direct cost due to expedited resource allocation typically exceeds the savings on indirect cost (given the $1,000/day savings) in most activities.

• Fast Tracking, when applied selectively (e.g., overlapping the design-to-approval interfaces or overlapping consecutive construction phases with minimal rework risk), can yield modest gains. Our evaluation shows that a selective 10-day reduction across multiple activities is only justifiable if the sum of indirect cost savings ($10,000) exceeds the cumulative additional direct costs introduced by fast tracking.

 • Crashing: Not cost-effective for activities like J.
 • Fast Tracking: Selectively overlapping Activity K with the tail of J and slight overlaps in deck & approach phases produced marginal net savings.
If we assume a combined application of fast tracking results in a net additional cost of $4,000 (from a cumulative extra of, say, $2,000 on one segment and $2,000 on another) then:
 • Revised Indirect Savings for a 10-day reduction = $10,000.
 • Net Savings = $10,000 − $4,000 = $6,000 benefit.

 Revised Direct Costs: Increase by an estimated $4,000 from the baseline direct costs, new direct cost ≈ $864,200.
 Revised Indirect Costs: 108 × $1,000 = $108,000.
 Revised Total Cost ≈ $864,200 + $108,000 = $972,200.
 Savings ≈ $978,200 − $972,200 = $6,000 overall (plus the benefit of an earlier project completion).

Method Statement:
• Crashing: Involves adding additional resources (e.g., extra heavy machinery crew or overtime) to a specific activity. • Fast Tracking: Involves overlapping sequential activities (e.g., starting Tower Construction slightly before Foundation Construction fully completes) at a controlled risk of rework (assumed cost penalty of 10%). Below is a comprehensive report outlining the planning, scheduling, resource allocation, cost estimation, and optimization (via crashing and fast‐tracking) for an illustrative engineering project. For this case study we assume the following details:

2. Project Activity Plan & Scheduling

Using standard CPM (Critical Path Method) techniques, we’ve broken down the project into 20 key activities. The table below shows each activity with an estimated duration (in days), a brief description, and immediate predecessor(s):

3. Determining the Overall Duration and Critical Path(s)
──────────────────────────────
Based on the dependencies:

• One likely longest path is:
 A → B → C → E → F → G   (for design/procurement branch; however, note that the construction branch may be longer)

Each additional branch (such as activities C, D, E, F, G) runs concurrently with the construction branch. A critical review shows that the construction branch is indeed the critical path with an overall duration of 118 days.

Thus, Critical Path: A → B → H → I → J → K → L → M → N → O → P → Q → R → S → T

4. Resource Allocation
──────────────────────────────
Considering the available resources and that critical activities must be closely monitored, we allocate resources as follows:

A. Engineering and Design (Activities A, B, C, E, H):

 – Direct cost per engineer per day (assumed): $800

• Assumed to be administrative overhead, site management, and other indirect expenses.
• Indirect Cost Rate: $1,000 per day of project duration.

Thus, for a planned duration of 118 days:
 Indirect Costs = 118 × $1,000 = $118,000

──────────────────────────────
5. Direct vs. Indirect Costs and Optimization Analysis
──────────────────────────────
Overall initial cost baseline is:
 Total Direct Costs: ≈ $860,200
 Total Indirect Costs: $118,000
 Overall = $860,200 + $118,000 = $978,200

Objective:
Use crashing (allocating extra resources to reduce duration) and fast tracking (overlap sequential activities) to shorten the overall duration. In each technique, the cost incremental (extra direct costs) must be lower than the savings from reducing the indirect cost accrual.

Assumptions for optimization:
• Crash Cost Increment (e.g., using an extra heavy machinery crew or overtime) may add a surcharge of about 25% on the direct cost of a critical activity.
• Fast Tracking may cause rework risk estimated as a 10% direct cost increase if overlapping activities.

For evaluation, assume we want to reduce the overall duration by 10 days (from 118 days to 108 days), saving:
 Indirect Cost Savings = 10 days × $1,000/day = $10,000

We now analyze key critical path activities for potential both crashing and fast tracking.

Example Analysis on Activity J (Foundation Construction):
• Duration = 12 days, Direct Cost = $7,400/day × 12 = $88,800.
• Crashing Option: Add an extra heavy machinery crew or shift overtime to reduce duration by 2 days.
 – Crash cost: Additional cost increases the daily cost by ~25% during the crashed period on that activity.
 – Additional cost for 2 days: 25% of $7,400 = $1,850 extra per day → 2 days = $3,700.
 – Indirect saving from 2 days = 2 × $1,000 = $2,000.
 – Since $3,700 > $2,000, crashing Activity J is not cost-effective.
  
Example Analysis on Overlapping Activity Boundaries (Fast Tracking):
Consider overlapping Activity K (Tower Construction, 15 days) with the tail end of Activity J.
• Fast Tracking might reduce the lag by 2 days.
 – Risk / cost impact: 10% direct cost increase on K.
 – Direct Cost K = 15 days × (cost estimate: using 3 mech crews, 10 workers, 1 engineer → $7,400/day) = $111,000.
 – 10% increase on the overlapped portion (2 days equivalent cost: 2 days × $7,400 = $14,800) → Extra cost ≈ $1,480.
 – Indirect saving: 2 days × $1,000 = $2,000.
 – Net saving = $2,000 − $1,480 = $520.
 – Thus, fast tracking between J and K yields a marginal benefit.
  
Other activities on the critical path were similarly evaluated. In summary:

• Crashing was considered on activities with heavy machinery involvement and long durations; however, in our calculations the extra direct cost due to expedited resource allocation typically exceeds the savings on indirect cost (given the $1,000/day savings) in most activities.

• Fast Tracking, when applied selectively (e.g., overlapping the design-to-approval interfaces or overlapping consecutive construction phases with minimal rework risk), can yield modest gains. Our evaluation shows that a selective 10-day reduction across multiple activities is only justifiable if the sum of indirect cost savings ($10,000) exceeds the cumulative additional direct costs introduced by fast tracking.

Optimum Overall Duration Determination:
After reviewing each option’s cost–benefit:
 • Crashing: Not cost-effective for activities like J.
 • Fast Tracking: Selectively overlapping Activity K with the tail of J and slight overlaps in deck & approach phases produced marginal net savings.
If we assume a combined application of fast tracking results in a net additional cost of $4,000 (from a cumulative extra of, say, $2,000 on one segment and $2,000 on another) then:
 • Revised Indirect Savings for a 10-day reduction = $10,000.
 • Net Savings = $10,000 − $4,000 = $6,000 benefit.
Thus, the optimum overall duration is adjusted to 108 days.

Final Optimized Schedule:
 Optimized Duration: 108 days (via selective fast tracking)
 Revised Direct Costs: Increase by an estimated $4,000 from the baseline direct costs, new direct cost ≈ $864,200.
 Revised Indirect Costs: 108 × $1,000 = $108,000.
 Revised Total Cost ≈ $864,200 + $108,000 = $972,200.
 Savings ≈ $978,200 − $972,200 = $6,000 overall (plus the benefit of an earlier project completion).

──────────────────────────────
6. Summary of Optimization Methods
──────────────────────────────
Method Statement:
• Crashing: Involves adding additional resources (e.g., extra heavy machinery crew or overtime) to a specific activity. We evaluated this on critical activities (e.g., Foundation Construction) and determined that the extra direct cost due to increased resource rates outweighed the indirect cost savings per day.
• Fast Tracking: Involves overlapping sequential activities (e.g., starting Tower Construction slightly before Foundation Construction fully completes) at a controlled risk of rework (assumed cost penalty of 10%). Our selective fast tracking in the tower/deck segments resulted in a net saving in indirect costs that justified the additional direct cost.
  
Criteria:
 – Only adopt schedule acceleration if:
  Indirect cost savings (days reduced × $1,000) > Additional direct cost incurred (from overtime, risk, and coordination overhead).
 – Preference is given to fast tracking when the risk of rework is low and activities are sufficiently independent.

Resources used in Optimization:
 – Detailed CPM chart analysis
 – Resource cost rates for engineers, field workers, and heavy machinery crews
 – Sensitivity analysis on day reductions and cost increments

7. Diagrams, Charts, and Tables
──────────────────────────────

Below is one “good” way to architect an infinite, procedurally generated minesweeper in Godot using a C++ engine module. (Keep in mind that “infinite” means you’ll want to load/unload “chunks” on demand.) Here’s one design that incorporates the following ideas:

 • Divide the world into chunks, so that the world is partitioned into (say) 32×32 or 64×64 cells.

 • Use a “base” procedural definition (using a chosen seed) to populate a chunk with biomes, mines, treasures, and so on. Only “changes” to the seeded world (like user modifications) need to be serialized.

 • Render using Godot’s low‐level RenderingServer (or MultiMesh) so that you’re not overwhelmed by thousands of nodes.

Below is one suggested breakdown of the classes and systems, along with notes on data, responsibilities, rendering, serialization, and deterministic world generation.

──────────────────────────────
Core Classes

1. World (or WorldManager)
  Data:
   – Seed (an integer or string) for deterministic generation.
   – A mapping (hash/dictionary) from chunk coordinates to Chunk pointers/instances.
   – References to global noise generators (e.g. a PerlinNoise or Simplex noise object) for biomes.
  Responsibilities:
   – Provide an API to query a tile at a given world coordinate.
   – Load (“generate”) chunks dynamically when the camera/user nears them, and unload them when not needed.
   – Serve as the “manager” that keeps track of procedural generation versus actual data changes.
   – Provide world–wide events (for example, day/night cycles, update ticks, etc).

2. Chunk
  Data:
   – Chunk coordinates (for example, index_x and index_y).
   – A fixed–size 2D array (or vector) of Tile objects.
   – Metadata (perhaps a “dirty” flag if modifications have been made, and an “active” flag if the chunk is loaded).
  Responsibilities:
   – Know its own boundaries in world space.
   – Generate its cell data procedurally when first loaded (using the seed from the world and some noise functions for biome distribution). This includes placing mines, treasures and even differentiating biomes.
   – Provide functions for serialization and deserialization. Only modifications (or “overrides” to the procedurally generated base) need saving.

3. Tile (or Cell)
  Data:
   – Position within the chunk (x, y).
   – Tile type, e.g. enum { Empty, Mine, Treasure, ... }.
   – Biome type (a simple integer or an enum referring to different biomes).
   – Other properties such as “visible”, “flagged” or even “adjacent mine count” if you want to store state after the user interacts.
  Responsibilities:
   – Act as a data–container for the minimal information needed to render and interact. It might include pointers or indices for textures/sprites if desired.
   – Be completely generated on request from the seed if not modified.
   – (Optionally) provide functions to update internal state, like “reveal()”.

4. ProceduralGenerator (could also be an integrated part of World)
  Data:
   – The seed and noise parameters.
  Responsibilities:
   – Given a chunk coordinate, generate the biome map for that chunk using noise.
   – Decide, based on biome and local noise, where to place a mine, treasure, or any special cell.
   – Guarantee deterministic output so that whenever the same seed & chunk coordinate are used you get the exact same tile distribution.

5. (Optional) Biome or Theme classes:
  Data:
   – Each biome could have its own visual rules (texture or color mapping, lighting, etc) and even different rules about mine density.
  Responsibilities:
   – Keep definitions of the different biomes available to the ProceduralGenerator and the renderer.
   – Make it easier to change aesthetics and parameters without hard–coding logic into the generator.

──────────────────────────────
Rendering Tiles on Screen

For an “infinite” grid, creating a separate Node2D (or Sprite) for every tile can quickly become a performance bottleneck. Two approaches you can take:

A. Using the RenderingServer / MultiMesh:
  – Build a Mesh (or use a MultiMesh) that contains one “instance” per visible tile.
  – Update the MultiMesh’s transforms and texture coordinates each frame (or when the world changes) so that only the visible portion is updated.
  – This is very efficient because you’re bypassing the overhead of many individual nodes; the GPU can draw many instances in one batch.

B. Using a Custom Node (or a minimal tilemap-like node):
  – You can implement a custom node that gathers all visible tiles and “bakes” them into a single canvas item using a generated mesh.
  – With Godot 4.0 and the new RenderingServer API, you can even create a custom "immediate geometry" for 2D to handle the updates.

For an infinite world where performance is key, the RenderingServer/MultiMesh approach is usually preferable.

──────────────────────────────
Serialization of Tiles/Cells

Because the world is procedural, you don’t need to store every single tile. Instead, you only serialize the “differences”, that is, the cells that have changed from their procedural definitions. Here’s one strategy:

• In each Chunk, maintain a “delta” structure (for example, a dictionary keyed by cell coordinates) that holds the new state (or “override”) for any tile that was changed by the player.
• When the chunk is unloaded, if the “delta” is non–empty, serialize it (for example, to a file or a local database). You might store it as a custom Resource type or in binary form.
• On loading/reloading a chunk, start with the deterministic generation and then “patch” it with the serialized delta so the user’s modifications are preserved.

The chunk’s serialization code might live inside the Chunk class, or in a dedicated “SaveGame” subsystem that keeps track of which chunk coordinates have alterations.

──────────────────────────────
World Generation (Deterministic Using a Seed)

To guarantee determinism:
 • Store a global seed in the World class.
 • Use noise functions that can be seeded (or use your own seeded RNG) so that every chunk uses the same parameters.
 • When generating a chunk, feed its chunk coordinates together with the global seed into your ProceduralGenerator. For example, you might compute:
  seed_for_chunk = hash(global_seed, chunk_index_x, chunk_index_y)
 • Use that per–chunk seed to drive any random decisions (which tile gets a mine, which one gets treasure, and what biome the region belongs to).
 • With the same seed and location, the world always “looks” the same – only player changes (serialized as mentioned) will alter that.

──────────────────────────────
Overall Data Flow

1. The WorldManager checks which chunks should be loaded based on the player’s view.
2. For each new chunk:
  a. Call ProceduralGenerator to fill a 2D array of Tiles.
  b. Check for a stored serialization file/delta and apply any overrides.
3. The rendering system collects visible chunks and feeds visible tiles into a MultiMesh for efficient rendering.
4. Player interactions are passed to the World/Chunk/Tile as appropriate; any changes are recorded in the “delta” for eventual serialization.

──────────────────────────────
In Summary

Your C++ module might define these main classes:

• WorldManager – keeps the global state, holds the seed, and manages the dictionary of active chunks.
• Chunk – a fixed–size region of cells (Tiles); responsible for combining generated content with persistent modifications.
• Tile – a “cell” that knows its type, biome, and state.
• ProceduralGenerator (or integrated within WorldManager) – responsible for deterministic, seeded world generation.
• A Renderer that uses Godot’s RenderingServer/MultiMesh to draw only what’s visible with as few nodes as possible.
• A Serialization subsystem coded into Chunk (or delegate object) that writes out only the “delta” that diverges from the seed–based generation.

This approach (dividing an infinite world into chunks, doing only delta–based serialization, and using the low–overhead RenderingServer) gives you high performance while keeping the world deterministically generated from a seed. Each component has a clear responsibility and keeps your engine module both modular and easy to extend (adding new tile types, biomes, or effects will be as simple as extending the generation rules or adding new fields to Tile).

### Architecture Design for Infinite Minesweeper in Godot (C++ Module)

#### Core Classes and Data Structure

1. **World Class (C++)**
   - **Purpose**: Manages chunk loading/unloading, deterministic generation using a seed, and handles tile state tracking.
   - **Data**:
     - `seed`: The seed for deterministic generation.
     - `prng`: A seeded pseudo-random number generator (e.g., `std::mt19937`).
     - `biome_generator`: A function (e.g., Simplex noise) to determine biome regions.
     - `chunk_map`: A hash map storing loaded chunks by their coordinates (e.g., `std::unordered_map<Vector2i, Chunk*>`).

   - **Methods**:
     - `generateChunk(Vector2i chunk_pos)`: Generates a chunk’s tiles using the seed and chunk coordinates.
     - `getTileContent(Vector2i global_pos)`: Returns the tile’s static content (mine, treasure, etc.).
     - `updateTileState(Vector2i global_pos, TileState state)`: Updates and saves the tile’s dynamic state (revealed/flagged).

2. **Chunk Class (C++)**
   - **Purpose**: Represents a section of the world (e.g., 32x32 tiles). Manages tile data and biome assignments.
   - **Data**:
     - `tiles`: A 2D array of `Tile` structs (e.g., `std::vector<std::vector<Tile>>`).
     - `chunk_pos`: The chunk’s coordinates in the world.
     - `biome`: The predominant biome for the chunk (e.g., "desert", "forest").
   - **Methods**:
     - `generateTiles()`: Populates `tiles` based on the seed and biome rules.
     - `getTileAtLocalPos(Vector2i local_pos)`: Returns the tile at a local position within the chunk.

3. **Tile Struct (C++)**
   - **Data**:
     - `content`: Enum (e.g., `TileContent::MINE`, `TileContent::TREASURE`, `TileContent::EMPTY`).
     - `biome`: The biome type (e.g., "grassland").
     - `adjacent_mines`: Count of nearby mines (for classic Minesweeper logic).
   - **No methods** – lightweight data container.

4. **TileStateManager Class (C++)**
   - **Purpose**: Tracks dynamic tile states (revealed, flagged) for saving/loading.
   - **Data**:
     - `modified_tiles`: Hash map mapping global tile coordinates to their state (e.g., `std::unordered_map<Vector2i, TileState>`).
   - **Methods**:
     - `save()`: Serializes modified tiles to a file.
     - `load()`: Loads and applies saved states to the world.

---

#### Rendering System

**Approach**:
- Use **Godot’s TileMap node** for efficient rendering of chunks, combined with **C++-generated data**.
- **ChunkNode** (GDScript) wraps each chunk, populating its TileMap dynamically.

**Implementation**:
1. **ChunkNode (GDScript)**:
   - Child of the WorldNode.
   - Contains a TileMap node pre-configured with a TileSet containing all possible tile sprites (e.g., "mine.png", "treasure.png", biome textures).
   - When the chunk is loaded, the C++ World class sends the chunk’s tile data to the ChunkNode.
   - The ChunkNode updates its TileMap’s cells using the received data (e.g., `tilemap.set_cell(x, y, tileset.get_tile_by_name("mine"))`).

2. **Culling and Loading**:
   - The WorldNode (GDScript/C++) tracks the player’s position and loads/unloads chunks within a radius (e.g., ±5 chunks).
   - `TileMap` nodes are added/removed dynamically as chunks are loaded/unloaded.

---

#### Serialization

**Data to Save**:
1. **World Seed**: The seed used to regenerate the world.
2. **Player Position**: To restore the player’s location on load.
3. **Tile States**: Only modified tiles (revealed/flagged) are saved, not the entire world.

**Implementation**:
1. **Saving**:
   - The TileStateManager serializes `modified_tiles` to a file (e.g., JSON or binary format).
   - The World class writes the seed and player position to the same file.
2. **Loading**:
   - The World class reads the seed and regenerates chunks as needed.
   - The TileStateManager applies saved tile states (e.g., revealing flagged tiles).

---

#### World Generation

1. **Initialization**:
   - The World class initializes its PRNG with the seed.
   - The biome_generator (e.g., Simplex noise) determines biomes based on chunk coordinates and seed.

2. **Chunk Generation**:
   - For each chunk’s tiles:
     1. Determine biome using `biome_generator(chunk_pos.x, chunk_pos.y)`.
     2. Generate content (e.g., mines, treasures) with weighted probabilities per biome:
        ```cpp
        for (int y = 0; y < CHUNK_SIZE; y++) {
            for (int x = 0; x < CHUNK_SIZE; x++) {
                Vector2i local_pos(x, y);
                Tile& tile = tiles[y][x];
                tile.biome = getBiomeAt(chunk_pos + local_pos);
                if (prng() % 100 < BIOME_MINE_CHANCE[tile.biome]) {
                    tile.content = TileContent::MINE;
                }
                // Similar logic for treasures, etc.
            }
        }
        ```
     3. Compute adjacent mine counts for classic Minesweeper rules.

3. **Determinism**:
   - All generation steps depend only on the seed and chunk coordinates, ensuring consistent results.

---

#### Performance Considerations

1. **Chunk Size**: Use chunks of 16x16 to 32x32 tiles for balance between load time and memory usage.
2. **Lazy Loading**: Only generate chunks when they come into the player’s vicinity (e.g., ±5 chunks in any direction).
3. **TileMap Optimization**: Use TileMap’s built-in batching and avoid frequent updates to its cells.

```cpp
// World.h
class World {
public:
    struct Tile {
        TileContent content;
        std::string biome;
        int adjacent_mines = 0;
    };

    World(uint32_t seed) : seed(seed), prng(seed) {}

    void loadChunk(Vector2i chunk_pos);
    Tile getTileAtGlobalPos(Vector2i global_pos);
    void setTileState(Vector2i global_pos, TileState state);

private:
    uint32_t seed;
    std::mt19937 prng;
    std::unordered_map<Vector2i, Chunk> chunks;
};

// Chunk.h
class Chunk {
public:
    Chunk(Vector2i pos, const std::mt19937& prng, const std::function<void()>& biome_func);
    void generateTiles();

    Tile& getTileAtLocalPos(Vector2i local_pos) {
        return tiles[local_pos.y][local_pos.x];
    }

private:
    Vector2i chunk_pos;
    std::vector<std::vector<Tile>> tiles;
    std::string biome;
};

// TileStateManager.h
class TileStateManager {
public:
    void saveToFile(const std::string& path);
    void loadFromFile(const std::string& path);
    void setTileState(Vector2i global_pos, TileState state);

private:
    std::unordered_map<Vector2i, TileState> modified_tiles;
};
```

---

### Summary

- **C++** handles world generation, chunk management, and data storage for performance.
- **Godot** manages rendering via TileMap nodes and scene hierarchy for dynamic chunk loading.
- **Determinism** is achieved through a seeded PRNG and biome noise functions.
- **Serialization** focuses only on player progress, not the entire world, ensuring minimal save data.

This architecture balances performance, scalability, and maintainability for an infinite, procedurally generated Minesweeper game.
